title: Strains & Sprains Overview
subtitle: Strains, Sprains, Tendinopathies & Bursitis of the Wrist

content.text: This lesson provides an overview of general strains, sprains, tendinopathies, and bursitis of the wrist. While specific conditions (like De Quervain's or TFCC injury) are covered in later modules, this overview covers the general principles.
Strains
Muscle strains affecting the wrist are not very common.
Tendinopathies
Tendinopathies affecting the wrist are not very common (other than the specific conditions covered in later modules — FPL tenosynovitis, De Quervain's, trigger finger).
Bursitis
Bursitis affecting the wrist is not very common.
Wrist sprains are the most clinically relevant general injury in this category.
Key Points

items: FOOSH injuries are very common and frequently lead to a palmar ligament sprain (either extrinsic or intrinsic) with or without fracture
FOOSH injuries commonly cause fractures and/or dislocations — these should always be ruled out
Overpressure in the direction that stresses the suspected ligament (flexion, extension, ulnar deviation, radial deviation) is the best way to assess for a sprain

content.text: Always rule out fractures and dislocations following a FOOSH injury before treating as a sprain.
Sprain Assessment
Overpressure in the direction that stresses the suspected ligament is the best assessment method:
General Sprain Grading

items: Grade 2 (Moderate): Laxity with a firm end feel
Grade 3 (Severe): Laxity with a soft end feel (possible rupture)

content.text: Treat as for general sprain management, following established rehabilitation principles.
General Sprain Treatment Goals

items: Promote a functional scar and reduce adhesions at site of injury
Restore neuromuscular control and resting muscle tone
Treat compensatory structures to restore overall function

content.text: Massage treatment for wrist sprains follows general sprain rehabilitation principles. The specific approach depends on severity, stage of healing, and individual assessment findings.
Your goals will always be based on your assessment findings pertinent to the individual you are treating. Severity and stage of healing will determine which techniques are appropriate.
Recovery timelines depend on the grade of sprain and adherence to protection/modification. Mild sprains typically recover faster than moderate or severe sprains.
Clinical Impression Format
A clinical impression for a sprain should include: affected ligament, severity, and stage of healing.

quiz.question: What is the most common mechanism of injury for wrist sprains?
quiz.explanation: FOOSH injuries are very common and frequently lead to palmar ligament sprains, with or without fracture.

quiz.question: What should always be ruled out following a FOOSH injury before treating as a sprain?
quiz.explanation: FOOSH injuries commonly cause fractures and/or dislocations, so these should always be ruled out.

quiz.question: In sprain grading, laxity with a firm end feel indicates what severity?
quiz.explanation: Grade 2 (Moderate): Laxity with a firm end feel. Grade 1 is pain without laxity, and Grade 3 is laxity with a soft end feel.
